entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer 14:1</reference> <div eID="gen13995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> The Uselessness of Prayer on behalf of the People. - The title in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer 14:1</reference> specifies the occasion for the following discourse: <hi type="italic">What came a word of Jahveh to Jeremiah concerning the drought.</hi> - Besides here, אשׁר היה is made to precede the דבר יהוה in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1">Jer 46:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.47.1">Jer 47:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.34">Jer 49:34</reference>; and so, by a kind of attraction, the prophecy which follows receivers an outward connection with that which precedes. Concerning the matters of the droughts. בּצּרות, plur. of בּצּרה, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, might mean harassments, troubles in general. But the description of a great drought, with which the prophecy begins, taken along with <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jer 17:8</reference>, where בּצּרת occurs, meaning drought, lit., cutting off, restraint of rain, shows that the plural here is to be referred to the sing. בּצּרת (cf. עשׁתּרות from עשׁתּרת), and that it means the withholding of rain or drought (as freq. in Chald.). We must note the plur., which is not to be taken as intensive of a great drought, but points to repeated droughts. Withdrawal of rain was threatened as a judgment against the despisers of God’s word (Lev 26:19.; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.17">Deu 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.23">Deu 28:23</reference>); and this chastisement has at various times been inflicted on the sinful people; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">Jer 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">Jer 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.10">Jer 23:10</reference>; Hag 1:10. As the occasion of the present prophecy, we have therefore to regard not a single great drought, but a succession of droughts. Hence we cannot fix the time at which the discourse was composed, since we have no historical notices as to the particular times at which God was then punishing His people by withdrawing the rain.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Jer.14.2-Jer.14.6">Jer 14:2-6</reference> <hi type="italic">Description of the distress arising from the drought. -</hi> Jer 14:2. <hi type="italic">Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish, like mourning on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goeth up.</hi> Jer 14:3. <hi type="italic">Their nobles send their mean ones for water: they come to the wells, find no water, return with empty pitchers, are ashamed and confounded and cover their head.</hi> Jer 14:4. <hi type="italic">For the ground, which is confounded, because no rain is fallen upon the earth, the husbandmen are ashamed, cover their head.</hi> Jer 14:5. <hi type="italic">Yea, the hind also in the field, she beareth and forsaketh it, because there is no grass.</hi> Jer 14:6. <hi type="italic">And the wild asses stand on the bare-topped heights, gasp for air like the jackals; their eyes fail because there is no herb."</hi> <div eID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> The country and the city, the distinguished and the mean, the field and the husbandmen, are thrown into deep mourning, and the beasts of the field pine away because neither grass nor herb grows. This description gives a touching picture of the distress into which the land and its inhabitants have fallen for lack of rain. Judah is the kingdom or the country with its inhabitants; the gates as used poetically for the cities with the citizens. Not mankind only, but the land itself mourns and pines away, with all the creatures that live on it; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.4">Jer 14:4</reference>, where the ground is said to be dismayed along with the tillers of it. The gates of the cities are mentioned as being the places where the citizens congregate. אמלל, fade away, pine, is strengthened by: are black, i.e., mourn, down to the earth; pregnant for: set themselves mourning on the ground. As frequently, Jerusalem is mentioned alongside of Judah as being its capital. Their cry of anguish rises up to heaven. This universal mourning is specialized from <reference osisRef="Jer.14.3">Jer 14:3</reference> on. Their nobles, i.e., the distinguished men of Judah and Jerusalem, send their mean ones, i.e., their retainers or servants and maids, for water to the wells (גּבים, pits, 2Ki 3:16, here cisterns). The <hi type="italic">Chet</hi>. צעור, here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.4">Jer 48:4</reference>, is an unusual form for צעיר, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>. Finding no water, they return, their vessels empty, i.e., with empty pitchers, ashamed of their disappointed hope. בּשׁוּ is strengthened by the synonym הכלמוּ. Covering the head is a token of deep grief turned inwards upon itself; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>; 2Sa 19:5. האדמה is the ground generally. חתּה is a relative clause: <hi type="italic">quae consternata est</hi>. "Because no rain," etc., literally as in 1Ki 17:7. - Even the beasts droop and perish. כּי is intensive: yea, even. The hind brings forth and forsakes, sc. the new-born offspring, because for want of grass she cannot sustain herself and her young. עזוב, <hi type="italic">infin. abs</hi>. set with emphasis for the <hi type="italic">temp. fin</hi>., as <reference osisRef="Gen.41.43">Gen 41:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.8.11">Exo 8:11</reference>, and often; cf. Gesen. §131, 4, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, Ew. §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. The hind was regarded by the ancients as tenderly caring for her young, cf. Boch. <hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. i. lib. 3, c. 17 (ii. p. 254, ed. Ros.) The wild asses upon the bleak mountain-tops, where these animals choose to dwell, gasp for air, because, by reason of the dreadful drought, it is not possible to get a breath of air even on the hills. Like the תּנּים, jackals, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">Jer 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.22">Jer 10:22</reference>, etc. <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. has <hi type="italic">dracones</hi>, with the Aram. versions; and Hitz. and Graf are of opinion that the mention of jackals is not here in point, and that, since תּנּים does not mean <hi type="italic">dracones</hi>, the word stands here, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.3">Exo 29:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.2">Exo 32:2</reference>, for תּנּין, the monster inhabiting the water, a crocodile or some kind of whale that stretches its head out of the water to draw breath with gaping jaws. On this Näg. has well remarked: he cannot see why the gaping, panting jaws of the jackal should not serve as a figure in such a case as the present. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Jer.14.7-Jer.14.8">Jer 14:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">The prayer. -</hi> Jer 14:7. <hi type="italic">"If our iniquities testify against us, O Jahveh, deal Thou for Thy name’s sake, for many are our backslidings; against Thee have we sinned.</hi> Jer 14:8. <hi type="italic">Thou hope of Israel, his Saviour in time of need, why wilt Thou be as a stranger in the land, like a wayfarer that hath put up to tarry for a night?</hi> Jer 14:9. <hi type="italic">Why wilt Thou be as a man astonied, as a mighty man that cannot help, and yet Thou art in the midst of us, Jahveh, and Thy name is named upon us - O leave us not!"</hi> <div eID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13998" type="x-p"/> The prophet utters this prayer in the name of his people (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">Jer 14:11</reference>). It begins with confession of sore transgression. Thus the chastisement which has befallen them they have deserved as a just punishment; but the Lord is besought to help for His name’s sake, i.e., not: "for the sake of Thy honour, with which it is not consistent that contempt of Thy will should go unpunished" (Hitz.). This interpretation suits neither the idea of the name of God nor the context. The name of God is the manifestation of God’s being. From Moses’ time on, God, as <hi type="italic">Jahveh</hi>, has revealed Himself as the Redeemer and Saviour of the children of Israel, whom He had adopted to be His people, and as God, who is merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and of great goodness and faithfulness (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>). As such He is besought to reveal Himself now that they confess their backsliding and sin, and seek His grace. Not for the sake of His honour in the eyes of the world, lest the heathen believe He has no power to help, as Graf holds, for all reference to the heathen nations is foreign to this connection; but He is entreated to help, not to belie the hope of His people, because Israel sets its hope in Him as Saviour in time of need (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer 14:9</reference>). If by withholding rain He makes His land and people to pine, then He does not reveal Himself as the lord and owner of Judah, not as the God that dwells amidst His people; but He seems a stranger passing through the land, who sets up His tent there only to spend the night, who "feels no share in the weal and woe of the dwellers therein" (Hitz.). This is the meaning of the question in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.14.8">Jer 14:8</reference></hi>. The ancient expositors take נטה elliptically, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.12.8">Gen 12:8</reference> : that stretches out His tent to pass the night. Hitz., again, objects that the wayfarer does not drag a tent about with him, and, like Ew., takes this verb in the sense of swerve from the direct route, cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.19">2Sa 2:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.21">2Sa 2:21</reference>, etc. But the reason alleged is not tenable; since travellers did often carry their tents with them, and נטה, to turn oneself, is not used absolutely in the sig. to turn aside from the way, without the qualification: to the right or to the left. סוּר is in use for to turn aside to tarry, to turn in, Jer 15:5. We therefore abide by the old interpretation, since "swerve from the way" has here no suitable meaning.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer 14:9</reference> <div eID="gen13998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13999" type="x-p"/> The pleader makes further appeal to God’s almighty power. It is impossible that Jahveh can let Himself look like a man at his wit’s end or a nerveless warrior, as He would seem to be if He should not give help to His people in their present need. Since the time of A. Schultens the ἁπ. λεγ. נדהם is rendered, after the Arab. <hi type="italic">dahama</hi>, to make an unforeseen attack, by <hi type="italic">stupefactus</hi>, <hi type="italic">attonitus</hi>, one who, by reason of a sudden mischance, has lost his presence of mind and is helpless. They are not therefore held excused because false prophets told them lies, for they have given credit to these lies, lies that flattered their sinful passions, and have not been willing to hear or take to heart the word of the true prophets, who preached repentance and return to God. Quod igitur ita rapiuntur homines ad imposturas, hoc fit eorum culpa, quoniam magis propensi sunt ad vanitatem, quam ut se Deo et verbo ejus subjiciant . To Hitz. it seems surprising that, in describing the punishment which is to fall on seducers and seduced, there should not be severer judgment, in words at least, levelled against the seducers as being those involved in the deeper guilt; whereas the very contrary is the case in the Hebrew text. Hitz. further proposes to get rid of this discrepancy by conjectures founded on the lxx, yet without clearly informing us how we are to read.
